[DOT]

With all due regard to
the joint committee on the Printing of Parliament, the last paragraph of their report need not be taken in consideration by the House as it relates to a matter which was not referred to the committee. Under the rules and customs of British parliaments, standing committees are not administrative bodies and * their power is limited by such orders or instructions as may be given the House. When the committee on Printing was formed the House passed the following resolution:
That the select standing committee on Printing be empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the House; and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
It is evident, therefore, that since the question of the orthography used in official documents by the various departments was not referred to this committee, it had no authority to report thereon and the last paragraph of the report should be struck out. When the House is called upon to give its concurrence I shall rule then that this paragraph is out of order.
I may add that the House is perfectly free to refer the question of official orthography to this or any other committee, but until it has done so, no committee has power to take it up and make recoramendations.
I most strongly hold, however, for the King's English, and it is quite proper that the various departments should understand that the standard English spelling should be used in official documents. If the matter had been referred by the House to that committee, then it would have been their duty to consider it. I say this in all fairness to the members of the committee who are doing their duty splendidly.

When we pass legislation of this kind we usually try not only to make it clear but also to make it enforceable. We are told that the purpose of the bill is to place this metal in exactly the same position that gold and silver occupy now. I have already pointed out that there are only two amendments, the first in the title and the second in this particular clause. There is an interpretation clause which, if anything is to be done, must be amended, because it deals with marks, and it is the improper marking which is the offence. In the original act we have in the interpretation clause the definition of "mark" as follows:
"Mark" means any mark, sign, device, imprint, stamp, brand, label, ticket, letter, word, figure or other means whatsoever of indicating, or of purporting to indicate, quality, quantity, or weight of gold or of silver, or quality or kind of gold or silver plate.
Then there is the definition of dealer:
"Dealer" means any person who is a manufacturer of, or a seller of or dealer in, whether by wholesale or retail, any of the articles to which this act applies; and whether such person is an individual person, or a corporate or unincorporated body of persons, or a director, manager, officer or agent of any such body.
Then section 3 provides that the act shall apply to (a) all gold articles; (b) all silver articles, (c) all plated articles. It is perfectly obvious, therefore, that if we are to deal with this matter intelligently and effectively we must also amend this section to make the act apply to platinum. What further consideration,
if any, has the minister given to the matter of erecting an internal storage elevator at Lethbridge? This question has been before *parliament, I think, year in and year out [DOT]for the last ten or twelve years, and the people of the district feel they are being treated very *unjustly in the distribution of these elevators, some of which have been placed at points not *nearly so well entitled to them as Lethbridge. *I discussed this matter at considerable length last year when the item for the Edmonton elevator was being considered, and the then Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) assured me that the representations made at that time would be fully considered-that the Grain Commission were going to investigate the Lethbridge situation. I inferred from the minister's statement that a report would be obtained with respect to Lethbridge and I knew that when it was presented it would be favourable. I therefore expected that some consideration would be shown to Lethbridge when the estimates were brought down this year.
I do not want to discuss the matter at great length but I draw the minister's attention to the fact that over 40,000,000 bushels of wheat which is about one-fourth of the entire production of Alberta, went through the Lethbridge freight district last year. I also draw his attention to the fact that such
5. p.m. an elevator is of great importance to us in connection with the movement of grain by the western route. It is true that we have an internal storage elevator at
Calgary but our easiest route to Vancouver is not through Calgary but through Golden. In taking the latter route some of t'he more severe railway grades are avoided. There are a great many reasons, both of a national and of a local character, to warrant the establishment of an internal storage elevator at Lethbridge. As I stated last year there is scarcely a place where difficulty <is more likely to ensue over car shortages than in that district. We are served by one railway solely, .the Canadian Pacific whereas Calgary, Edmonton and other points are served by two or three distinct lines of railway, and have the benefit of all the freight car equipment of those several lines. Since I have been a [DOT]resident of that part of the country we have suffered very severely 'indeed from car shortages on a number of occasions, in spite of the fact that the Canadian Pacific is handling the business in a very efficient and capable way.
I can remember that as far back as 1915 we were unable, on account of car shortages and lack of elevator space, to get that year's crop out until the summer of 1916. Last year we had a crop quite equal to that of 1915, and we had a similar crop in 1916. In 1922 we had a crop of 22,000,000 bushels of wheat, over one-third of the entire crop of Alberta. We feel very much aggrieved over the slight we have experienced 'in this matter, and our people are insisting that action be taken. A number of years ago when the location of these internal Storage elevators was first before the country and under consideration by the Grain Commission, Dr. Magill recommended the building of an internal storage elevator at Lethbridge. He was at that time head of the Royal Grain Commission. Since I have become a member of this House, I have talked with Dr. Magill several times and he has assured me that he made the recommendation at that time. He asserts, as he did then, that Lethbridge is the logical point for the establishment of one of those elevators. There come to Lethbridge, if I recollect aright, lines from seven different directions. There is the line from Macleod from the west; the main line of the Canadian Pacific from the east; the Cardston branch; the Coutts branch; the Lethbridge-Weyburn branch, recently completed, which brings grain from eastern Saskatchewan through to the west coast; the Al-dersyde branch; the Macleod-Calgary branch; and very soon we are to have constructed by the Canadian Pacific the Kipp-Retlaw branch. All these lines run into Lethbridge and bring an immense quantity of grain into that centre.
Supply-Grain Elevators

One special reason why they want an internal storage elevator there is the avoidance of a car shortage, which is a very important matter, because in the fall when our shipments of grain are heaviest, there is the greatest call on our railways for the shipment of coal. It takes 200 to 300 cars a day during that part of the year to get coal out of the Lethbridge district. The railways very properly will give preference to the coal business when the weather happens to be cold on the prairies and the people are likely to suffer from inclement weather.
Last year I had a statement, to which I referred, from the Lethbridge Board of Trade which is very greatly interested in this subject, especially on account of the mixed farming operations which we are trying to carry out in that district. They have gathered extensive data regarding the advantages which will be derived by that section of the country from the building erf an internal storage elevator at that point, and I am going to cite some of the figures. They state that in 1922 the wheat production was 22,662,000 bushels. We are very anxious to have the screenings left in that district in order to feed our sheep as we have a largely developed sheep industry there and have shipped as high as 1,750,000 pounds of wool per year. That has been very important at seasons when on account of drought conditions, the wool product was about the only immediate source of money for the farmer to provide for necessities and to leave any money at all in that part of the country. If we figure the screenings alone at two per cent on that wheat crop it *would amount to 453,000 bushels of screenings, or 13,597 tons. When you figure the cost to the farmer of shipping this quantity of waste all the way to Fort William and to the sheepmen in order to get the same quantity of screenings back-and pay S15 to $20 a ton for them in addition-you will realize that it amounts to a good deal of money. They paid $67,986 freight on those screenings im 1922. It required to move those screenings alone 302 cars. It required to move the whole wheat crop 15,108 cars, if we take 1,500 bushels of wheat per car. If you make the same calculation in connection with this year's wheat crop of 40,000,000 bushels, you have almost double the result. You have 800,000 bushels of screenings with a freight loss on those screenings alone of $120,000. The byproduct which they want to use in the Lethbridge district is carried all the way to Fort William, and then when they want those screenings in order to fatten their sheep in the winter season, they have to have the stuff

shipped all the way back again. That is what happens, and is one of the strongest arguments in favour of the erection of an internal storage elevator at that point with full facilities for screening grain.
That is only one feature of the matter. It is figured, if I remember aright, that it takes about 100 days to fatten sheep, and about 250 pounds of those screenings together with other feed must be used. The calculation is that with the screenings from the 22,000,000-bushel crop of 1922, they could fatten 76,000 more lambs per year than they are doing at the present time. On the basis of the 40,000,000-bushel crop for this year, those figures would be very nearly doubled. There you had in 1922 a possibility of adding 76,000 sheep to those that the people in that district are able to handle, worth $8 a head and, for mutton, this would mean $600,000 more to the return of the sheep men of that section. Every one of those sheep would yield probably seven to eight pounds of wool, or a total of about 500,000 pounds, which even at the low price of 25 cents a pound, would amount to $125,000. Therefore, the extra amount which could actually have been produced for the sheepmen of that district if they had the screenings alone there, would have been about $725,000. This is a matter of public interest to this country. The clothing situation and the food situation of this country are affected by it, and advantages would accrue to the people generally as well as to the farmers.
I want to urge this upon the minister. I notice he is paying no attention to what I am saying.
I am making notes of what my hon. friend is saying.

I thank the minister. That is only one feature. I have always contended, as our people have that the Lethbridge district which produces as good grain as can be found anywhere in the world, should be the centre of an immense milling industry; that our raw product should there be converted into flour and feed of various kinds. There is no reason why that should not be the case.
I was before the Grain Commission years ago in connection with this subject when Dr. Magill was inclined to favour Lethbridge as the place where one of those elevators should be established and which he subsequently recommended. I took the ground that Lethbridge and the southern Alberta district should be the Minneapolis of Canada, and I hope the day will come when that will be the case.
I have been assured that the millers in that district are ready, the moment an internal storage elevator is erected there, to double and

Supply-Grain Elevators
treble their capacity. Time and again I have been in the offices of the Ellison Milling Company there and I have been shown files, telegrams and messages, of various kinds containing orders for flour from Japan and China. This country is very much interested in developing the oriental trade. In order to manufacture that flour the millers must have the lower grades of wheat, 4, 5 and 6, out of which they make it, and they cannot retain the quantity of these low grades of wheat in that part of the country under the present system of handling the crop and shipping it to Fort William, to supply that trade and keep their mills running to full capacity the year round, further develop the industry, and give our people the full advantage of the crops which they produce. I was on the coast last winter on the invitation of the Vancouver Harbour Commission and one of the first things I noticed on the docks was a lot of flour from the Ellison Mills of our district being loaded for the Orient. When I got home I spoke to the manager of the milling company, Mr. 'George Green, in regard to what I had seen. There were five carloads of that wheat being loaded on a vessel in the harbour at that time and I so reported to him; he said that if I had waited two or three days longer I should have seen thirteen more carloads. That is the situation and I think it is important enough to call for the consideration of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We can increase our output for the oriental and foreign trade from two or three times if we can get ah internal storage elevator out there which will retain in our district enough of the different grades of wheat year by year to supply our mills.

What is the
present milling capacity?

I cannot say offhand. There is another thing I want to bring to the attention of the minister in that connection. At great expense to the people there are being developed extensive irrigation areas in that part of the country, and the method of farming in these irrigated districts is of the intensive type. We should be, and are, fast developing along dairy lines, raising hogs and cattle and sheep and poultry; and it is especially essential to the welfare and the proper development of these districts that we should have, combined with the forage crops which are easily produced in large quantities on the irrigated lands, the byproducts from our mills. There is scarcely a year in which we are not compelled, in order to supply the demands of our dairy farmers, to ship into that country bran and shorts
and all sorts of mill feeds and screenings which should be produced right there in the immediate district. It might be of some importance to the minister to mention the fact that one of our big sheep men there has brought down to Fort William, and fattened on the screenings, as many as ten thousand sheep in a single band. Mr. Harvey, a prominent sheep man of Raymond, Alberta, has brought that number down on different occasions; and a number of other men have brought down bands numbering from 2,500 to 5,000. Can the minister not do something to meet this situation? It is a long-standing demand which is justifiable from every angle I have mentioned: from the car shortage and the milling standpoint, from the mixed farming and live stock standpoint, and from the standpoint of the oriental trade. There is every reason why the minister should seriously consider this matter and bring down in his supplementary estimates a sum sufficient to enable him to begin the construction of an internal storage elevator at that point.

I realize that this is a matter
of great interest to my hon. friend (Mr. Jelliff), and I agree with him in many respects. There is no doubt that many new elevators both internal and at various ports are required. But my hon. friend recognizes I have no doubt, that the government is obliged to cut its coat according to its cloth; we must proceed cautiously in matters of public expenditure and therefore cannot build more than one or two elevators each year. The hon. member knows that the cost of erection of these elevators must come out of current expenditure, and at present we are endeavouring to lighten the taxation burdens of the people as far as possible. During the recess it is my intention to devote myself to an intensive study of the whole wheat ques- i tion, with the purpose of finding some solu- l tion if possible to the problem of cheaper I marketing of the wheat of the prairie pro- \ vinces. I realize that a margin of two, or three, or five cents a bushel means much to those provinces, and with a crop of 400,000,000 or 500,000,000 bushels a reduction of five cents would amount to a considerable sum. The matter is worth inquiry. The department over which I preside can do no greater service to the people of the West than to endeavour to work out some amended system which will enable the wheat grower to market his wheat at a lower cost than is possible to-day. With that object in view I intend to devote to the whole subject as much time as I can between the close of this session and the opening of the next. I fully agree that it is a
Supply-Grain Elevators

sound idea to have in the immediate locality of the farming district an elevator where screenings-and if a mill-where by-products from the flour can be obtained for cattle. One thing we try to do in the milling business is to export as much flour as possible, retaining at the same time for the benefit of the farmers of this country all the by-products from the mill. For about three or four months of the year there is a great shortage of shorts and bran and certain other byproducts. If we can obtain a greater volume of export business in flour in Canada it will help us to supply this shortage, because feeds are rarely exported. I shall be glad to take into consideration the remarks of my hon. friend when the question of marketing western wheat is under scrutiny.

When I was at Vancouver last winter I attended a banquet given by the harbour commission at which a gentleman connected with the milling industry of that city stated, in the course of his address, that Vancouver was not likely to become a big milling centre because it did not have a sufficient number of live stock in that part of the province to consume the by-products. He mentioned that it would be a great help to the milling industry of Canada, and would facilitate the handling of the grain crop, if more storage elevators were erected in the interior, and he named Lethbridge specifically.
I was glad to learn something from the figures which the minister gave the committee last night as to the results from the internal storage elevators. I find that the storage elevator which was erected at Calgary showed a loss in only one year, and that the net profits during the years quoted, 1915 to 1924, were $374,488.77. The elevator at Moose Jaw showed net profits of $170,782 for the same period. I am inclined to think that those elevators are most needed in the Alberta country, for we are furthest from Fort William and from Vancouver, and the empty cars that finally trickle back into our neighbourhood are accordingly fewer and very much slower in getting to us than to others more advantageously located. Consequently we have more trouble in meeting our car situation than those who are in the other provinces, and we have greater occasion to use these storage elevators. The minister also mentioned the elevator at Saskatoon, which I noticed made a net profit, in round figures, of $370,000. I think that is a good investment for our people. It is not a gratuity to the grain growers, because eventually these ele-
vators pay their way. We are very hopeful that an interior storage elevator will be established at Lethbridge, especially in view of the mixed farming that is carried on in the district, for this would guarantee a better return than is usual where this condition does not prevail.

I understand they are all on Hansard, so I will look them up.

Is it the intention of
the government to instal drying machinery in the Edmonton elevator? And would it be feasible to get a through freight rate on grain originating east of Edmonton and destined for Vancouver? At present we have to pay the local rate to Edmonton plus the local rate from Edmonton to the coast.

Answering the first question,
it is intended to equip this elevator with all the machinery required including adequate drying facilities. In reply to the second question, freight rates are under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

Supply-Grain Elevators

I was very much interested in what the minister told us as to an effort to be made to bring down the cost of marketing grain, and also to hear his statement that efforts were to be made to export flour instead of grain.

The mere fact that we were
able to get the ocean rates on flour from Canadian ports equalized with the rate as from American ports has helped wonderfully.

I was going to
say that I hope it is to be something more than a pious wish. Of course the discrimination which was practised in connection with the Atlantic movement to which my hon. friend's reference applied, was so bad that I do not suppose anjmne thought it would continue. If my hon. friend did anything to get rid of it I congratulate him.
He did.
It was simply a scandal.
I was able to draft such a plain clause that the gentlemen at the Economic Conference understood it, and we succeeded in getting the rate equalized with the American basis.

I suppose the
object of the ministers's last statement is to show that he knows something more about dollars and cents than he knows about platinum.

No, something more than I
know about law.

The correction of those rates is not helping the flour business very much while the present spread continues. We had evidence the other day before the committee on Railways that the present spread between flour and grain is 7 cents. It is hard to believe that we are seriously trying to promote the export of flour if we are going to sit down quietly under such a spread as that. The old spread was at one time as low as half a cent. It went up a cent, then a cent and a half, then to three cents. The government became alarmed-that was in 1913, I think-at the spread having doubled. I remember taking the matter up with the British Board of Trade when in England, and I recall that the whole question was gone into pretty thoroughly by that body. No definite action was taken by them, however. My recollection is that at that time the spread was 5i cents; to-day it is 7. That means there is just that much disability standing in the way of what the minister says ought to be done. We ought 216
to export a maximum amount of flour, for the reasons pointed out by the hon. member (Mr. Jelliff). It ought to be done in the interests also of the dairying industry, because those engaged in that industry are compelled to import hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of foodstuffs in order to carry on their dairying activities.

Wheat is one of the best ballasts that can be obtained, and consequently the vessels very often take it at an extremely low rate. The ocean rates are something over which we have little control; they are under the direction of an Atlantic shipping conference. We have at present a gentleman in England, Mr. Preston, investigating these matters.

I quite understand that in certain cases we do get grain carried at a nominal rate. I am only sorry that that is not done more often, and that that nominal rate does not work back to the producer. It is not within his power to take advantage of these adventitious contracts. But the question of spread has nothing to do with these accidental rates.
I do not know much about platinum, but I know a little about flour and wheat. What is the spread to which my hon. friend refers? Is it the spread between certain commodities?
No, the spread between the rates on wheat and on flour, a matter that has been discussed in this House and everywhere else for years.
My hon. friend had not made any reference to wheat or flour.

I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I thought I had. The spread I refer to is not that which applies in the case of abnormal rates or rates made applicable for the purpose of trimming boats; it is the spread between the regularly quoted rates, the conference rates, of wheat on the one side and flour on the other. If my hon. friend finds that his representative in England does not do something, well, he is going over himself and perhaps he will take a turn at it. Of course, some spread is to be expected; that must be said in fairness, because there are claims for damages, and there is a little more money involved in the case of loading and unloading flour. But the present spread is certainly a matter which should receive attention.

Does my hon. friend suggest a remedy?

I would refer
the minister to the report of the committee on Agriculture last year and to the evidence taken before that committee on this very question. At one of the imperial conferences a committee was appointed to take this matter up, and' a report was made two and a half years ago dealing with the question and suggesting, as I recall it, the creation of a tribunal in that connection. Nothing has been done by the government on that report. Perhaps they can find some better way of handling it, but certainly we shall never get anywhere unless we try to do something definite in connection with this question of spread.
I am already trying.

I hope my hon. friend will not weary in well doing. Perhaps he will be able to bring back something for us next year. May I ask the minister whether he thinks there is any more favourable centre than Lethbridge for the purposes of an elevator of this kind, having regard to the character of the country and to the fact that we have there a district which can only live if mixed farming is adopted to a greater degree and if there are enough screenings there for the purposes of feed to the necessary stock? I have not heard any particular reason why Lethbridge was overlooked when others were being built. There may have been some reason, but the minister has not given it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understood that Lethbridge was to go before Calgary at one time.

I do not know;
I am only looking for information.
It certainly should have pre^ ceded erection of an elevator at Moose Jaw.

Is that not a point where there is really more chance for mixed farming, and for the sort of thing the Minister of Agriculture wants done? Is there no better point at which to start it? I would like to find out from my hon. friend what the milling capacity is at Lethbridge. As I understand it, a lower quality of flour is in demand for the markets of the Orient than for the European markets. We use for milling for the Orient grades 4, 5 and as low as 6. That, of course, makes a flour of a character that does not carry as well, and would not last as long, as flour from our No.
1 hard, and it is not worth as much. It would look to me as if it was in the interest of economy that that should be milled as conveniently to Vancouver as possible.
I suppose that my hon. friend knows that low grade flours are also made from No. 1 and No. 2.
I think there is a smaller proportion of low grade flours made from the more expensive grades.
It also depends upon the particular patent.

I think I am
right in saying that we have a maket for our poorer grades of flour made from the lower grades of wheat in the Orient, and if I am right in that, it would also follow that it would be the course of wisdom to mill that at some point in western Canada that is convenient to the Vancouver gateway. It would seem to me there is a great opportunity just now to extend this milling business in the Orient, particularly in Japan at the present time, for obvious reasons. Is the minister in a position to say whether we have sufficient milling capacity at the present time? Does he not think it would be a good thing to have a multiplication of our milling activities? I think the hon. member for the district suggested three times as much.

The milling business increased almost too rapidly during the war, and the situation of the milling market to-day is that many mills find themselves in the position of running only twelve hours a day. I suppose my hon. friend knows that it is utterly impossible to make a flour mill pay when it operates only twelve hours a day, for the very simple reason that to operate for the other twelve hours costs only a trifle more. When the mill operates for only twelve hours all the overhead and almost every charge carried when operating twenty hours must be carried just the same. Operating at night simply means an addition to your staff of a couple of packers and a couple of millers only, say in a mill with a capacity of five hundred barrels. You would only require four extra men, but you could double your capacity. When the mill is working only twelve hours, an inferior flour is turned out because the run is stopping and starting again in the morning, and that is a bad thing. The longer the mill continues to run steadily, the more uniform and better the grade of flour turned out.

I entirely agree with my hon. friend, but he is speaking of the situation generally. I was speaking having regard particularly to the milling of the lower grades of wheat for the markets of the Orient, and the best geographical position for mills

for the purposes of that trade. My hon. friend is quite right as to the situation generally, but I was wondering how we were situated to-day having regard to the number of mills established in the district where it would be cheap and economical to handle the lower grades of flour through Vancouver to the markets of the Orient. The reason I asked is that the hon. member for the district pointed out that if the terminal elevator were built there, the local millers apparently think they have such a demand for their flour in the Orient that they are prepared to instal three times as great a capacity as they now have.

The great problem in operating a flour mill is that the lower grade flour brings a very low price, and consequently there is some question whether a mill could operate entirely on low grade flour. The territory to which my hon. friend has referred seems to commend itself to me as a very good point for a flour mill.

I would like to again press the point of freight rates to the internal elevators. The internal elevators have mostly shown a loss, and I do not think the farmers know exactly the cost to themselves of turning in their wheat to the terminal elevators. The charge in some cases, perhaps, is too high. The farmer, of course, would like to use the nearest elevator possible, so that he may get his weights and grades and go to the bank and get his money, but he does not know what the extra charge will be when his grain is turned in there.

There is no extra charge, so far as the shipping of grain through the Edmonton elevator is concerned, except one cent a hundred, the usual charge for stopover. You can ship from any point and obtain the through rate to Vancouver with a stopover at Edmonton, at a charge of one cent a hundred for that stopover, whether it is for cleaning or any other purpose.

Would that apply also to
wheat destined for Fort William? Would it apply to wheat going to the terminal elevator at Saskatoon and loaded at some point east of Saskatoon?

I venture to say it applies to
all. I might quote my own case. We have a stopover privilege at Fort William. We can ship to Montreal, and we have a stopover at my home town. It costs us on the all-rail route one cent, and lake and rail, three cents.
That cent a bushel stopover does not include elevator charges? It is simply for the stopover.
That is all.

Is there no charge for
spotting cars in addition to that? When you re-spot your car to ship out, are you not charged for that also?
M,r. LOW:	No, unless it is going out by
another line, and it is some distance from the other. In my own case, between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, there is a switching charge of $5.

Yes.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Acting Postmaster General):
speechtext:
We discussed
the situation yesterday with the representatives of the postal employees and the newspapers last night intimated what the results of that discussion were. Before saying anything about that, may I say that before the executive left Toronto there was an order issued apparently for a strike yesterday at five o'clock, which would be effective throughout Canada. The executive, however, after discussions in Toronto, came here to discuss the situation with us yesterday. We appeared to be reaching an agreement in the neighbourhood of five o'clock, but whether the executive were late in forwarding their message to Toronto or not at all events the Toronto employees went out-all the postal workers in the offices and their assistants, all the mail carriers and their assistants, and the chauffeurs. Of course when that happened it broke in upon our negotiations. The government, as was intimated in the press, offered full consideration of the claims of the post office employees; we proposed that after the claims of the Civil Service were all adjusted by the Civil Service Commission we might sit around a table and discuss thoroughly the complaints of the
Postal Employees

post office employees as well as the complaints of any other civil servant. In addition to that we suggested that in the case of employees whose revised rates as determined by the Civil Service Commission are less than the former rate plus the 1924-25 bonus, such bonus shall be continued until the salary revision for the entire service has been consummated. That in brief was the offer of the government, and up to five o'clock we had hopes that it would be accepted by the officials. For further consideration of the offer of the government they ordered their men to delay the strike for twenty-four hours. That order was not obeyed in Toronto nor was it obeyed in Montreal. Subsequently some of the men came back to work, but in Toronto they did not return. That was the situation up to ten o'clock last night, when the officers of the association left here to go to Toronto.
As hon. gentlemen well know, the busy hour of the day is about five o'clock in that city, which is the biggest centre perhaps, that is seriously affected. The mails come in about that time and there is heavy sorting to be done for distribution as well as the getting of the mails out on the trains. That was all delayed last night. At ten o'clock last night I felt that we could not delay any longer, and as there did not appear to be any hope of getting an adjustment in time to begin work upon the Toronto mailing, I issued instructions to the Toronto postmaster that if the men did not return by ten o'clock standard time this morning he was to proceed to' put on men to take their places. That was done and I had a report at about four o'clock that indicated we had almost in the neighbourhood of four hundred employees at work in the post office at Toronto. So far up to the moment we have not, except in Montreal and in some of the other centres, had to resort to putting men on. The negotiations went on throughout the day in Toronto between the executive and the post office employees there, but at five o'clock the result was that they were not able to persuade the men to return to work. One of the officers-the representative from Hamilton, I believe-in disagreement resigned and intimated that he would undertake to try to prevent the men from going out in the city of Hamilton. I have no further word on the situation except that at the moment the men in Toronto, that is the regular employees are out. They are out in London to a considerable degree; they are also out in Windsor, in Belleville, in Brantford and part of them in Montreal.
As to the western situation we have word 
from a number of centres, namely, Calgary, Edmonton, Saskatoon-most of the large centres-and there is no indication at the moment of a strike occurring. I am given to understand that there was not complete unanimity of feeling about the matter in these centres. We have no further word from Vancouver or Victoria; they took no action. Of course word reached them much earlier in the day than it reached the city of Toronto. At Montreal the mails are being moved, and everything was going on to-day except at one postal station in the city where a little trouble developed this morning. In the Maritime provinces, with the single exception of Moncton, the officers were operating with full staffs. At any rate there was no intimation to the department that they intended to go out on strike.
What the result will be of the issuance of the order coming at five o'clock to-night I am unable to say, but I wish to restate what I said the other day in the House when speaking on behalf of the government: While I am a strong sympathizer with labour,
6 p.m. while my sympathies are with the working man-as I think, perhaps, is the case with most of us-it is the government of Canada that is concerned here and it must carry on the business of the country. I said to the representatives of the men the other night "Gentlemen, my sympathy is with you up to the point where you declare a strike. After that bear in mind that I will exercise all the ingenuity and energy I possess to carry on the business of Canada." That is my feeling in the matter. At the moment we have nearly four hundred new employees at work in the Toronto post office. It is said that while the light holds out to bum the sinner may return. At the same time I simply have to say to the men that a settlement cannot be postponed indefinitely. The postal service of Canada must be carried on, the mails must be moved; and so far as I am able I am going to take every legitimate means to secure the number of employees necessary to do that. I make no threats. As I say my sympathy is with the man who has to work in that kind of way for a living. But there is a higher interest to be considered and that is the interest of the country at large. When that interest is attacked in that kind of manner my sympathy in very large measure ceases. Speaking on behalf of the government that is what I propose to do, so far as is possible, in order to keep the mails moving.

I wish to put two questions so that the House and the country may be informed; I have no desire to embarrass the

government in any way. What proportion of the total staff in Toronto is represented by the 400 men engaged, and have they been given the promise that they will be retained in the office in the event of a settlement?

that the grain can be carried by water he is speaking of the St. Lawrence route when navigation is open there.
Not necessarily so.

Then will my bon. friend
tell us what he means?

When the St. Lawrence
route is open I believe very little if any grain will go through either St. John or Halifax. It would be preposterous to carry grain by rail 700 miles, and in the case of Halifax
Supply-Grain Elevators

843 miles, when it can be carried the same distance by water for one-eighth the cost. Is there any force of appeal to patriotism that would induce shippers to go to that extra expense ?

I might answer that by reading a letter which I wrote Sir Henry Thornton, the president of the Canadian National Railways, and his reply. The following is my letter to him:
As you are no doubt aware, we have had under consideration for some time the matter of the erection of an elevator at Halifax.
There seems to be a difference of opinion among the grain men and others as to the wisdom of building an elevator at this port. In the estimates last session we made provision for an amount to enable the government, if found advisable, to commence the construction of an elevator at this point. However, before undertaking this large expenditure, we desire to know absolutely whether it is in the best public interest. I am therefore writing to ask you to let me have your frank personal opinion on this matter as soon as possible.
He replied on February 21, 1924, as follows:
Replying to your inquiry of February 15th, with reference to the proposed elevator at Halifax, briefly put, the following represents my view of the position.
The elevator referred to is of a terminal character and it is my understanding that it will be built and operated by the government-not by the railway. The railway has however recommended the erection of the facility as the present elevator has entirely outlived its usefulness.
Having regard to the long haul to St. John and Halifax, it is doubtful if there is any profit to the railway company in handling grain to either port. But this commodity is required by steamships at both ports partly for ballast and partly as cargo, and consequently an elevator at both ports would seem to be justified.
Bearing in mind the legislation recently enacted making Canadian ports attractive to import business, principally from Great Britain adequate and modem facilities for handling grain at Halifax would appear to be necessary for the protection of steamship service, and therefore a situation is created which is beneficial to the country as a whole.

What is the date of
that letter?

My letter and the reply are
dated respectively February 15 and 21 of this year.
I thought the government had decided on this matter long ago.

When I came into office I had before me all the information, but I endeavoured to ascertain the opinion of the president of the National Railways, knowing that he would give me, his views frankly. I have read to the committee just what he wrote to me.

Last year I believe the
amount of grain handled at this port was either 300,000 bushels or 300-I have forgotten just what the figure was.

If the hon. member proposes to discuss this matter I wish he would make himself acquainted with the facts. Neither 500 nor 300 bushels is correct; the hon. member's figures are absolutely wrong. Let him get the facts before he undertakes to discuss the matter.

If there is anything wrong about the figures I have, the responsibility must rest with the Department of Trade and Commerce because these figures were certainly contained in the report of that department.
I challenge the hon. member's statement and call upon him to produce the' figures. If he will submit the facts I shall be content to accept them; but his statement is absolutely incorrect.
I shall be pleased to do so.

The elevator facilities at Halifax are inadequate for the handling of the grain. I really do not know whether there is any grain going through the elevator or not; it may be going direct from the rail to the ship.
If there is no grain going through Halifax the elevator would handle it all right. W'hat does the minister mean when he says that he does not know whether or not there is any going through?
They are no longer discharging where the elevator stands.
Oh, is that the reason?
There is no elevator handy now to handle the grain.

Does the minister think
it is good policy to spend large sums of money carrying grain over the railway for the purpose

Supply-Grain Elevators
of providing ballast for the ships? Does he think we should compel the railways to carry the grain for nothing? I infer from the remarks made yesterday that it is the intention to compel the railways to carry the grain a part of the way for nothing; that is to say, they are not to be permitted to charge more for carrying the grain to Halifax than they charge for carrying it to Portland. That of course does not apply to the American railways. Now, this simply means that the National Railways will be obliged to carry grain hundreds of miles for nothing. Is that fair to those who are paying the bill? The Canadian people as a whole will have to pay for all this, and it does not seem to be a wise policy to take money from the public treasury or out of the producers of grain in order to make possible the transportation of wheat to Halifax to provide ballast for the ships.
Does my hon. friend think that the railways even at a reduced rate will lose money?

If the railways are carrying grain to Portland a distance of 297 miles at a fair rate-and we may assume that they are not getting more than a fair rate-then if our railways are compelled to carry it 843 miles for the same price, is that not sufficient evidence for my hon. friend that our railways will have to carry the grain part of that distance for nothing, and must therefore lose money?
No, it is not.

Either they are losing
on the one or they are getting an enormous profit on the other.

My hon. friend should
bear in mind that there is other traffic besides wheat, and that the success of the railway depends on the traffic it gets both ways, from east to west, as well as from west to east. The steamship companies with which the Canadian National is doing business give the railway a large inward traffic at Halifax, and if for the benefit of those ships that must get ballast wheat is carried, you will have to take into account the cost of the carriage of that wheat in connection with the profit from the cargo on the westward voyage. That trade is being developed by the ships calling at Halifax, and last year it was double that of the year before. It is like a grocer selling sugar on which he does not make any profit in order that he may sell some other commodity on which he does make a profit.

Would the minister apply
that to the National Transcontinental and the port of Quebec? Strange to say, the cost of carrying grain from Armstrong, north of Fort William, to the city of Quebec a distance of 960 miles, is 21 cents, whereas the cost from Calgary to Fort William is 154 cents or for 960 miles is 11 or lli cents. The rate from Winnipeg or from Fort William to Quebec is the same as to Montreal.
Oh no.

I think if my hon. friend has
facts and figures bearing on this he should produce them before contradicting my statement. I have looked into the matter and know.

Grain is carried by the rail
and water route for very much less; it is carried down to the bay ports for about 3 cents.

I am talking of the all rail
rate.

The rates on grain all rail
from Fort William to Montreal or to Quebec are the same; by lake and rail they are somewhat less to Montreal.
Half a cent a bushel.

It is more than that-four or
five cents. But from Montreal to Quebec the local freight rate applies, which amounts to about 10 cents per 100 pounds. Of course, if you ship by water during the navigation season you have the advantage of the lower rate. But when you have to ship all rail, or lake and rail from the bay ports-because the elevators there fill up during the fall and you are able to continue shipment by rail through the winter-there is a very slight difference.

But why is it that the grain is carried for such an excessive price from Fort William? As I pointed out before, while the rate from Armstrong to the city of Quebec is 21 cents, for the same distance, 960 miles, the through rate on the Canadian Pacific from Calgary to Fort William is 11 or 114 cents; that is, it is just double.

Double from where?

Twenty-one cents a bushel
from that place to Quebec, a distance of 960 miles. I had read that statement, and I inquired of the author if it was absolutely true, and he assured me it was.

That would verify my
figures.

A very slight difference.

But we are anxious to keep our grain in Canadian channels, and it seemed to me strange, particularly last fall when there was so much congestion on the lakes and trouble in getting our grain down at reasonable rates, that there should be this prohibitive rate from Armstrong to the city of Quebec, where we have an elevator with a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels only partly used. Now, the government can take this course if they wish in order to divert grain to Halifax, they can place an elevator there, but it is forcing the traffic uphill, it is the wrong place for it to go. I would be willing to vote money for Halifax for any legitimate purpose, for I should like to see the port built up,-
Thank you.

here last night by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), which I assume are correct, namely, Montreal to Halifax, 843 miles.

The minister told us last
night that the charge against the handling of the grain from western Canada was about 6i per cent on the facilities erected for handling that grain. When the Minister of Railways says that grain is needed at Halifax for ballast, to what department would he charge the construction of this elevator?

It would be charged to the Department of Trade and Commerce and come out of current account. We cannot discuss this question from one angle only, otherwise we do not get at the real essence of it. During the past year, as a result of the new arrangements or the development of old ones, the Canadian National has had connection with increased steamship landings at Halifax. If it be necessary for these steamers to have wheat ballast, is it not better to work that in through Halifax, retaining the trade with the steamships and encouraging the steamships to call at that port? It does not cost the grain producer any more, and in the final analysis it will not cost the railways much more. It is worth while to make these experiments.
If arrangements are not made by which outgoing ships can get cargo as ballast, what will be the result? If the Canadian product is all carried to Portland, which is the shorter route, then the traffic will not in every instance be over the National Railways, because once you get to Portland there is competition, whereas at Halifax the Canadian National has the advantage. We cannot fairly discuss the matter without taking into consideration these various aspects of it-the traffic east and west, the circumstances with respect to return haul, the local traffic, the development of the harbour,of the port, and so on-not particularly, perhaps, the development of the port, but the consideration that when ships are induced to call there the resulting traffic will bring good returns to the Canadian National Railways. That traffic, if developed properly, would overcome anything that might be lost in the hauling of the wheat to Halifax.

Hon. gentlemen in this

However, I did not rise for the purpose of taking exception to what my hon. friend said. Western Canada is just as anxious for the upbuilding of eastern Canada as it is for the development of any other section of the country. I believe the farmers there are ready to send their grain to the East at any moment if a satisfactory rate can be granted. The desirability of this was pointed out last night in a very brilliant speech by the Minister of Railways. Let me mention a few things in which the West feels that it is not getting a fair deal, not as a result of the action of any particular section of the country but owing to the operations of certain interests in Canada. I would refer first to what took place in parliament two years ago when we. discussed the Crowsnest pass agreement and were successful in having the price of grain brought within the terms of that agreement. The western farmers thought that meant a considerable advantage and anticipated saving quite an amount of money on their crop that year, but the result was not what they expected. The vessel owners on the lakes immediately raised their rates and swallowed up the benefit the western farmers expected to have derived by virtue of the Crowsnest pass agreement. I

believe I am safe in saying that the western farmer in consequence received practically nothing from the reduction under the Crows-nest pass agreement. Now, in matters of this kind regard should not be paid to one section of the country. I must say that
when I saw this vote in the estimates for the Halifax elevator I was considerably disappointed. The project has been a live issue for a long time. It has been greatly talked about, and many promises have been made in regard to it. All these seemed to have come to a focus in December last when it was expected the elevator positively would be constructed at once. This view seemed to be justified seeing that tenders were called for and offers received, and apparently only the return of the Prime Minister from England was necessary to close the bargain and proceed immediately with the construction of the elevator. At that time $200,000 had been voted, the same sum that now appears in the estimates. But nearly seven months have elapsed and we are told by the minister that the plans have not yet been decided upon. Practically nothing has been done we are given to understand, and the matter is still under the consideration of the 9 p.m. government. Under the circumstances but one conclusion can be arrived at in my opinion and that is that
the government are playing with the subject. There is no intention on their part to erect an elevator at Halifax until another election looms up. Then we shall have one built in the air, so to speak, and it will melt in the sunshine. That is no way to conduct public business: It is not the way to treat any portion of the Dominion. Notwithstanding the treatment accorded to Halifax we see the sum *of $1,000,000 in the estimates this year for an elevator at Edmonton-following a vote of $200,000 last year-and how much more will be demanded next year none of us can tell. As so much storage is required for the grain out there in the West, which grain has to be moved east or west after it is placed in that elevator, why should the Canadian National Railways not provide in the eastern section of the country facilities for the handling of that grain? In the winter time water transportation which my hon. friend (Mr. Millar) spoke about, is out of the question. The rail rates to the Atlantic coast from Halifax on the north to, I think I can say, Baltimore on the south, have been equalized. The rate on inland carriage from points of production to the ocean is the same to all those ports. If that be the case, if the railways have established that principle, why should my hon. friend be so concerned about carrying the grain! to Halifax, which is, I admit, somewhat farther east than ports farther south?
There is another point which, perhaps, he has not thought of. If the land carriage to Halifax is longer than to either St. John or Portland, that certainly shortens the ocean carriage, and would it not be a reasonable proposition that the steamer which carries the grain the shorter distance from Halifax to the Old Country should reduce her rate for ocean carriage somewhat below the rate from St. John, Portland, New York, or any of the other Atlantic ports? The saving of time to a steamer would be greater, and we all know that time in connection with shipping is valuable. That would be a reasonable proposition and, if adopted, would give the inland carriage that much greater advantage.
We have heard a great deal about Canadian business going through Canadian ports. That is a policy which I think this country should adopt and should begin at once putting into effect. It is not, perhaps, for me to suggest how that is to be done. It is for the government to work out a policy which would be for the benefit of this country as a whole. Vancouver, it is true, has lately attracted a good deal of attention in connection with the shipment of grain. From what we hear and read, that business will increase there, and we are very glad to know that it will, because until

Item agreed to.
Inquiry re ocean freight rates, $10,000.

I would direct the attention of the minister to the excessive freight rates charged on cattle shipments to the Old Country. The figure still remains at $25 a head to Dundee and $20 to other British ports. Since the lifting of the cattle embargo against Canadian cattle the farmers of this country have been encouraged to increase the production of cattle for this trade. The tendency to increase herds of this type has however received a serious setback by the excessive charges levied in ocean transportation, and unless these cattle can be shipped at something like $10 a head the farmers may as well abandon all idea of participating in any way in this valuable branch of agricultural exportation. This is not a western matter only; it affects nearly every province in Canada. In its general effects the export trade of cattle is of even greater value to the country than the exportation of wheat because the raising of wheat for export purposes can only be carried on successfully in districts that are peculiarly suited to its production. But the raising or finishing of cattle for export can be carried on, on almost every farm in Canada. Therefore this is a very serious problem and deserves the most careful attention of the government.
If it is not possible to bring ocean freight rates down to a reasonable figure, the farmers may as well be informed of the fact so that they will not continue to waste their resources and their energies in an endeavour to produce cattle for export. The crux of the problem is to find out what it costs to transport cattle to the British markets. It has long been asserted that freight can be transported seven miles by water at the same cost as one mile by rail. The correctness of this assertion is shown by the fact that freight can be shipped from Montreal to

Vancouver by the Panama all water route, over 7000 miles, and then east to Regina, another 1100 miles by rail, at a lower cost than by rail from Montreal to Regina, a distance of 1780 miles. The conclusion therefore is unavoidable that where there is competition ocean rates are approximately one-seventh railway rates. But in the transportation of cattle from Winnipeg to British ports we find that the charge to Montreal is about one-half of the charge for carrying the same cattle across the ocean. In other words, the ocean rate is twice that of the rail rate, although before the war it was less than one-half. Since 1914 railway rates on cattle have increased 40 per cent, while ocean rates have increased 166 per cent, and this in spite of the well-known fact that a great portion of the world's shipping is now lying idle. If these ocean rates on cattle are justified by the cost of service, the sooner the farmer finds another export market the better; otherwise his only alternative is to abandon his efforts to raise cattle for export. But the suspicion is widespread that these rates cannot be justified and that the business of transporting cattle to Great Britain is in the grip of a relentless combine. It is to be regretted that the Imperial Shipping Committee presided over by Sir Halford Mackinder was not empowered to investigate this situation thoroughly. It is undoubtedly the duty of the government to get at the facts. It has been suggested that in order to determine the cost of transportation, and to maintain our cattle trade with Great Britain, the Canadian government should charter ten or a dozen steamers suited for the purpose, and transport Canadian cattle at pre-war rates. Now, the Canadian farmer is not asking that this trade be maintained at the expense of the taxpayers generally; that would not be fair I am sure. But if the government were to engage in this traffic for a while in the manner suggested, the feasibility or otherwise of maintaining this trade on a profitable basis would be demonstrated.

In reply to my hon .friend, I
may say that Sir Halford Mackinder was advised that we wished the ocean rates on cattle to be investigated. With this in view we communicated with the Board of Trade, the city council, and other prominent men of both Winnipeg and Montreal. At the present time this very important matter, along with others, is receiving the attention of a special representative in England, and I hope during the recess to investigate the matter myself, because I fully realize that nothing will help agriculture more than to ensure to the farmer

a larger return from, his cattle than he has been receiving for the last few years. Before the session closes I hope to demonstrate in a practical way that I am trying to do something in this direction and I will then place before parliament the proposals I have in mind in order that hon. members may decide whether they should be adopted.

Is the minister convinced that the export cattle business cannot be carried on at the present transportation rates?

I had several meetings in this country with the representatives of the vessel owners and on each occasion they stated that it was utterly impossible to lower the rates, pointing out as one reason that the costs of dock-handling were as high as the peak during the war, and they informed me that the men were making a demand for a further increase in wages.

We very much appreciate the statement of the minister and look forward with some hope at least to a successful termination of his efforts. In endorsation of the remark by the hon. member for Selfkirk (Mr. Bancroft) I would point out the remarkable increase in cost and what it implies. The raising of the British cattle embargo brought a feeling of relief and inspired a good deal of hope in the hearts of the farmers, but I am afraid they have found that that embargo was only removed in order that a freight embargo might be substituted. The increase in transportation costs has been almost incomprehensible to us. Before the war cattle were carried from Montreal to English ports at an average ocean rate of $7.50 per head; since the war and at the present time the rate is $20 to the western ports and $25 to the eastern ports of England-an increase, as my hon. friend said, of 166 per cent.

Yes, in pre-war times.
Now, we quite understand that marine costs have risen since pre-war days, but we cannot believe that they have risen proportionately to any greater extent than railway costs of operation. There are fewer men employed in connection with ocean transportation, and in many ways the expenses are less than those incurred by our railways, and therefore I cannot see why the ocean rates should be any higher 218
in proportion than railway rates. At the present time it actually costs $10.20 to move a 1,200-pound1 steer-which is about the average for export-from Winnipeg to Montreal, a distance of 1,411 miles, while to move the same steer 2,060 miles by water costs from $20 to $25. In other words, the rates are almost the same per mile by water as they are by land. It is well known that water carriage is infinitely cheaper than land carriage, so that this state of affairs is to my mind unjustifiable. I cannot believe that these rates can be justified by the costs invilved. As I say, we are looking forward with some hope to a real improvement in these conditions through the negotiations and investigations being carried on and through the efforts of the minister and his department. If the present embargo on our cattle to the United States continues and if the present freight embargo to Great Britain continues, our live stock industry, the most important in the whole country, will be destroyed.
