Now, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the government cannot escape responsibility in regard to this matter. When they anticipated the raising of the embargo on Canadian store cattle in the Old 'Country the shippers of western Canada in a live stock meeting held at Regina in 1921, passed a resolution advising the government to take under immediate consideration the feasibility of getting some of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships to carry cattle overseas. Mr. Arkell, the live stock commis-218J
sioner, was present at that meeting, and he made the statement-I have it here, but I will not read it-that he understood there was a surplus of cattle-carrying boats, and knew for a fact that some of them were being dismantled at that time. Notwithstanding that, when the trade developed and the cattle were ready for shipment overseas, we were met with the situation that the shipping interests claimed they did not have space enough, and they immediately raised the carriage charges, which leads us to believe that there is a deliberate combine existing in order to extort the last dollar out of the Canadian farmer and the shipper of cattle. I would just like to quote a few words from Mr. Rice-Jones, who represents the Grain Growers' Grain Company, which ships 25 per cent of the cattle shipped out of Canada. He appeared before the Imperial Shipping Committee at Winnipeg and declared that the present steamship rate was almost prohibitive and was strangling the export trade between the two countries, Canada and Great Britain. This is a live question out in the West, and it also should be, and I believe is, in the East. Here is an extract from an editorial appearing in my own paper in Portage la Prairie, which expresses it in better language than I could use. Referring to a meeting held in Winnipeg about two months ago it says:
At the Stockers and Feeders banquet in Winnipeg eminent men like the president of the C.P.R. and 1st vice-president of the C.N.R. gave advice favouring mixed farming and cultivating the home market. This is what the boys call "old stuff." Reduced transportation rates is one of the greatest essentials to assist agriculture. It has been demonstrated that it costs more to transport a steer to the British market than it costs to buy the beast in the stockyard in Winnipeg. How is it possible for agriculture to succeed working on that basis?
I shall not keep the committee any longer to-night, except to sound this warning, unless we receive redress, and receive it very soon, the cattle raisers of Canada will have to go out of business unless we can find another market, because the Old Country market is not proving what we expected it to be.

The minister told us that the special agent was Mr. Preston. I would like to get his initials, and to know something of his occupation, and if possible, the terms upon which his services as special agent have been secured by the department.
His initials are W.T.R.

That name has ravished my ears before.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
What are his special qualifications for this investigation? What does he know about the business?
I have not the slightest doubt that he is qualified to carry on the investigation, and I hope that good results will follow.
When did he leave?
About six or eight weeks ago.
Had the Liberal organization given him leave of absence?

I do not understand why my
hon. friend interjects these questions. He knows very well that Mr. Preston has no connection with the Liberal organization, and has not had for a number of years. I cannot understand why a gentleman of the standing of the leader of the opposition should ask such questions.
It is strange.
It is.
What was his occupation before he went on that trip?
He is investigating the matters I referred to.
What was his occupation before?
I have no knowledge of what he was doing before. I knew he was quite capable of carrying on this investigation, and that is all I was concerned about.
Was not his principal occupation before hanging around to get the job?
You seem to know more about him than I do.
I know that.

I know he is a good man to carry on such an investigation, and I asked the government to put through the following order in council:
The committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, advises that W. T. R. Preston be employed to investigate the alleged discrimination in freight rates covering Canadian shipments from Atlantic seaports, and also regarding the alleged combine in connection with such shipments in marine insurance, and to report on these subjects to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
What date was that?
The 28th of February, 1924.

I have endeavoured to find out what his occupation was before he took
fMr. Meighen.]
this work. It strikes me that it would be very desirable to know whether he knew something of these very questions he was going to investigate, discrimination in freight rates, and freight rates in general. Perhaps he has that qualification, but so far as I know he has not, and I would be glad if the minister would let us know whether he has or has not.
I have already stated that I thought he was one of the best men in the country to investigate such questions.
He is a journalist or something of that kind, is he not?

It does not make any difference. I suppose lawyers are often appointed to investigate different matters. I imagine my hon. friend would say a lawyer was a good man to investigate matters in connection with the Grand Trunk railway. I am sure that a printer has some qualifications for such work.
Is that what he is, a printer?

This is not the first
step the government took towards meeting the situation?
It is mot the first step we took towards meeting what situation?
What preceded that?

When the delegates were going to England last fall I prepared a memorandum for them, pointing out that there was a discrimination against Canadian ports in the shipment of flour. I am sorry the exMinister of Finance is not in his place tonight because I think he made the remark that the difference did not amount to very much.

This is in relation to
flour. I mean in relation to cattle.

In relation to cattle? The
negotiations opened up about the same time.
As this?
Yes.
That is 28th February?

I think it was a little earlier
than that. I think I carried on negotiations Shortly before that.
With whom?

With the vessel owners in
the city of Montreal and elsewhere. I had several meetings with them at which I endeavoured to persuade them to reduoe the rate, but I was unsuccessful. However, negotia-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
tions are still going on and I purpose visiting England during the summer. That is one of the objects of my visit. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) made the statement this afternoon that an equalization of rates between New York and Liverpool, and between Montreal and Liverpool, would not amount to very much. Well, the equalization amounts to about five cents a hundred, about ten cents a barrel, and about two cents on every bushel of wheat. My hon. friends can quite understand that if the Canadian miller is at a disadvantage of two cents a bushel it is a great handicap to him. We succeeded in having the rates equalized, and I think my right hon. friend will admit that was a great accomplishment. At any rate the farmers, as well as the millers, will admit that, because if the average miller was sure of a profit of ten cents a barrel on flour the year round he would be well satisfied. It is the great volume of flour that is manufactured that tells, and the mill must be run the whole twenty-four hours or it is almost impossible to make a profit in milling. I do not know whether I have given my hon. friend all the information he asked for.

Now give us the terms on
which he was employed?

The gentleman who was sent
to England to investigate this matter? I will quote from the order in council:
The committee, on the same recommendation, further advise that subject to instructions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and while employed on the above work, Mr. Preston be paid remuneration at the rate of fifteen dollars ($15) per day for each day actually employed on the said work; and also that he be allowed for the time necessarily spent in travel while carrying on such work a living allowance not to exceed an average of ten dollars ($10) per day, in addition to actual cost of transportation while so employed.
There is no limit as to time?
No.
Does the minister expect that Mr. Preston will require the $10,000 appropriation, or is some of that to be used elsewhere?

Some of it has already been
used elsewhere. The chairman of the Imperial Shipping Committee was invited to visit Canada in connection with this investigation and we agreed to pay the actual expenses of the British visitors. Some of this vote will be used for that purpose.

Perhaps it would be
convenient for the minister to let us have
the particulars as to how this estimate is made up-how much is set apart for Mr. Preston and how much for the other purpose?

There is no portion set apart
for the other purpose.

Perhaps it will not be
enough?

The amount was arrived at
after the estimates had been prepared. We were not sure just how much would be required so w'e estimated the figure at $10,000. If I remember rightly I think the expenses of the gentleman referred to amounted to $2,000.

Will the minister
say whether there is any other provision made for taking care of Mr. Preston during the coming year?
For what?

Whether there is any other item in the estimates to take care of Mr. W. T. R. Preston during the coming year? The sum of $10,000 would surely not be sufficient. If this is the same W. T. R. Preston that I have in m'ind, I think he was acting in the inquiry into the freight rates on the lakes during the past summer.

He acted as secretary to the
commission.

And prior to that
he was employed by the government in the Old Land. I have here some references to Mr. Preston which date back to 1898. I believe that almost continuously since that time he has been paid for acting in a somewhat similar capacity to that in which he will act during the coming year. This thing is getting threadbare. I do not believe the minister really knows Mr. Preston's record, and his ability to have items appear in the estimates for his particular benefit.
Put him on annual salary.

The minister has
ability to size up the situation himself without any advice from Mr. Preston.

I have not had time; he is
preparing material for me.

Then all I can say is that if there is not time, and it is necessary to have someone make this inquiry, select some person whose reputation will bear investigation; do not appoint a political hack such as this, a discredited political hack, a man whose very reputation stank in tha

Supply-Trade and Commerce
nostrils of the people of this province during the last twenty-five years. I doubt if there ever was in the history of the province 'of Ontario, or the Dominion of Canada, a man who had a more unsavoury reputation than this Mr. W. T. R. Preston. I noticed the present member for West Elgin (Mr.McKilLop) sitting in his seat a few minutes ago and I asked him what year it was Mr. Preston was carrying on his operations in that constituency. There were two or three by-elections there inside of two years, in 1898 and 1899. The result of Mr. Preston's activities in that constituency was that the candidate of the Liberal party was elected, but when a recount took place it was found that more votes had been cast for that candidate than there were voters, in some of the polling divisions. An investigation was held and the Liberal who had been elected, Mr. Donald McNish, resigned his seat and protested against the methods which had been adopted. I have here a telegram that was sent out by Mr. Preston to Mr. McNish on the night of the election in that year. It reads as follows:
Heartiest congratulations. Sorry to the bottom of my heart cannot be with you to-night. To be supported by such a noble army of workers should make you the proudest man in Ontario.
This was the telegram that Mr. Preston sent to Mr. Donald McNish, the member who was supposed to be elected on that night. When the matter was investigated Mr. McNish resigned his seat and he had a statement published over his own signature as follows:
1.	That a large number of persons were specially sent into the constituency by men working on behalf of the Liberal party for the express purpose of taking part, on Mr. McNish's behalf, in the election held January 12, 1899, and we believe that fraudulent and corrupt means were used by some of such persons to secure his election.
2.	That several of the said persons illegally and without authority acted as deputy returning officers at the said election,-
That several of the said persons illegally and without authority acted as deputy returning officers at the 6aid election, and in at least three cases so acted in the names of reputable local men, having under assumed names, been introduced to the returning officer by local agents of Mr. McNish.
3.	That in many of the polling subdivisions of the riding there were grave irregularities connected with the return of ballot-boxes and their contents, the voting, and the counting of the ballots thereat.
4.	That there were large numbers of persons brought into the riding for the express purpose of personating legitimate voters, and, assisted by some of Mr. McNish's local supporters, such persons did personate qualified voters in voting for Mr. McNish.
5.	That the declared number of votes for Mr. McNish largely exceeded the number of bona fide votes cast for him.
That a large number of ballots cast for Mr. Mc-Diarmid were in some nefarious and corrupt manner

manipulated, whereby the result of the election was rendered doubtful, and that in this connection the voting at Shedden and Middlemarch, and in several divisions in St. Thomas, where said strangers so acted as deputy returning officers, merits special mention.
This is from Hansard of July 26, 1899, reporting the discussion in the	House of
Commons. This matter was threshed out upon that occasion and Mr. Preston was immediately appointed as an immigration agent in the Old Country in connection with the Department of Immigration and Colon ization. While in that capacity he got into touch with the provincial Director of Colonization at Toronto, and this matter was also placed on the records of this House two or three sessions ago. In view, however, of Mr. Preston's renewed activities and his ability to have the government provide for him, I am going to read some of the methods which he was advocating at that time. This letter was dated and written on government stationery from 17 Victoria Street, 'London:
W. T. R. Preston to the Director of Colonization in the province of Ontario:
I have your letter of a late date on emigration to Ontario. You incidentally say in the letter that you are opposed to indiscriminate emigration. Well, in that respect you agree with everybody else. I do not know any one who suggests, or who would propose, that there should be indiscriminate emigration to that province. Whatever is done must be done carefully, and any who are sent out must be well selected emigrants. But don't run away with the idea that only well to do people, or those with money, are going to emigrate. If you are going to keep up a population in the old parts of the province you must be satisfied with sober, energetic and industrious emigrants. I know all you people are terribly afraid of the foreign element. Upon that point I don't agree with you and have no hesitation in saying that a good class of foreigners scattered about the old parts of Ontario will do very much more towards preserving a proper agricultural population than those from England for instance. Politically speaking I believe the introduction of a hundred families or so into some of those close ridings with the connection which could be had and maintained here would easily preserve for us many doubtful seats in that province. I know the anxiety or nervousness of the minister upon this question. Confidentially, I may tell you, I fear it bears some slight resemblance to one of courage. You know enough about politics to know that courage always beats. However as we don't agree upon that phase of the question we won't discuss it.
I have heard from the Wallaceberg people in answer to my letter of the middle of last month and I am now trying to meet their wishes among the best growers of Belgium. I will be over there in the course of a week or ten days and will then write to you as also to them, upon the outlook there.
Yours very truly,
W. T. R. Prestox.
This letter was dated October 18th, 1901. Afterwards a good deal was heard-and some hon. members may recall this-about him and his connection with the notorious North Atlantic Trading Company which was subsidized by the government of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that time, and when an inquiry was demanded, the information was refused to parliament at that time, on the ground that some of those connected with that company were people of high standing on the continent and that some of them would likely commit suicide should their names be divulged. Mr. Preston was one of those who were associated with that scheme, and this has been the case during all these years. During the past year Mr. W. T. R. Preston was secretary of the commission that was investigating freight rates on the lakes. Now he is going to be taken care of by the vote that is before the committee to-night in order to provide for his maintenance. He evidently has claims upon hon. gentlemen opposite that he insists upon having recognized. He is not the only one. I have referred, during this session and last session, to some other parties who evidently contend that they also have claims that must be recognized and who< have been drawing their salaries and expenses out of the coffers of this country, illegally, as it was stated last session. The government absolutely refuse to grant a fiat to enable suit to be brought to recover the salary that had been paid to this other party. I claim that an item of this kind appearing in the estimates, with the minister stating that a portion of it, at least, is to go to pay for the services of Mr. W. T. R. Preston, is an item that ought to be struck out of the estimates. This country cannot afford to employ people of that character, discredited political hacks* that have been a barnacle upon the Liberal party in the province of Ontario for the last twenty-five years. It is about time that we were dropping characters of that kind instead of reviving them. I do not believe the minister knew the character of this man or he would not have made the statement he made here to-night, that this man was to draw the major portion of this $10,000 item which is now before the committee. This is the first time that I have referred to Mr. Preston's operations in this House, although they have been referred to frequently by others. I know there are many members in the House who know nothing about Mr. Preston, but the minister can very easily obtain the information that he desires without this item at all. If this item is merely to provide for Mr. Preston, under the guise of performing a public service then it should not appear in the estimate at all.
I absolutely refuse to be drawn again to-day into a debate of mud-slinging and the style of debate that one would expect to hear from political wardheelers when a campaign is at its height.

I object to having any insinuations thrown across the floor of the House. I came into the House a few minutes ago and I found that the minister himself was referring to Mr. W. T. R. Preston. You cannot introduce the name of Mr. Preston in this House and expect to avoid anything of this kind.

My right hon. friend himself
referred to Mr. Preston. Why should two or three gentlemen condemn Mr. Preston? There are other members of the House who may have an entirely different opinion of him.

What does the minister
think of the letters, which he has heard read, signed by Mr. Preston?

To tell you the truth, I did
not listen to them.

Then why does the minister describe something that he knows nothing about?
Mr. LOW" I heard enough of the remarks that were made in regard to the letters to know what they were about.

The minister expects to
appoint a character like this at the expense of the country and have no one make any remarks about him? If so he quite fails to realize the character of hon. gentlemen in this House. This money is nothing but a piece of jobbery against the people of Canada; there is absolutely no justification for sending Mr. W. T. R. Preston to England to report on cattle rates-a man who has had no more to do with matters of this kind than anybody whom the minister might pick out of any newspaper office in this Dominion, or off the street. Mr. W. T. R. Preston is a man who ever since the election has been hanging around the door of the Liberal party wanting jobs all the time and getting them whenever the government could hand them out.
Did my right hon. friend never have men hanging around looking for jobs?
Yes, but we did not give them.
You did not?

We did not send political hacks to England, at a cost of thousands of dollars to the people of this country, to look into questions in respect of which they had no experience whatever, no information and no qualification of any kind. A more absurd selection could scarcely have been made in the Dominion; I doubt whether the minister could have made one less acceptable to the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
farmers of Canada or to the people generally. Every one knows W. T. R. Preston. There is not a better known-or rather I should say a worse known-name in the political history of Canada. The minister may be going over to England this summer. Very well; let him go over and look into the matter. But do not send Mr. Preston over on the excuse that he is going to prepare the way for the minister. I find in the Speech from the Throne at the opening of the House a statement which in the light of what is revealed to-night is more than amusing:
As a stimulus to stock-raising in the Dominion, and of direct benefit to agriculture, the government has been endeavouring to obtain a lower carrying charge on all shipments of Canadian cattle.

Does the hon. gentleman object
. that?

I think it is really amusing that the government should see fit to put that passage in the Speech from the Throne, on the basis of the facts revealed by the minister to-night. What were the efforts that were to be made? The first effort was for the minister to see some of the shippers and ask them to reduce the rates. He failed; and the next effort, the only other one, was on the very day the Speech from the Throne was delivered, to pass an order in council to send Mr. W. T. R. Preston to England.

Does my hon. friend not know
that the negotiations had been carried on for several months?

The minister told us
what they were. He told us that he himself failed in his request of the shipowners to reduce the rates; he told us that he was in Montreal with a view to having this done. This failure of the minister and the appointment of Mr. W. T. R. Preston are worthy of insertion in the Speech from the Throne!

The efforts of the Minister of
Trade and Commerce were not, but the object was worthy of reference in the Speech from the Throne. Does my hon. friend know that almost every farmer in Ontario and in the province of Quebec, besides many in Alberta, have from six to ten steers to sell every fall?

Who is talking about
that?
If we can accomplish something in lowering the rates will it not help the agriculturists of the country?

Does the minister think that is the point I am making?
{Mr. Meighen.]
I know my hon. friend is trying to make out that what we are going to do is all wrong.

What I am making out
is this, that the order in council appointing Mr. W. T. R. Preston to go to England, the day the speech from the Throne was delivered, is no basis for the presentation to parliament of a document of this kind. The thing is to laugh! Undoubtedly the subject itself is of paramount importance and warrants the visit of the minister to England. It is big enough, and if the minister accomplishes anything we will give him due credit upon his return. The minister claims to have already spent some time on the subject. He evidently will have to spend a little more before he knows as much about it as hon. gentlemen who have spoken to my left to-night, and behind me as well. He does not know very much yet about it. Nevertheless, he does know something about business and about freight in general, and it is quite right and proper that he should go and look after the matter. But we object to providing an excuse for keeping in some measure of comfort a political refugee of the Liberal party. It does seem to me extraordinarily strange that since the embargo was removed about a year ago, and during the very time these supposed efforts were put forth to reduce the rates, the rates should go up to the alarming figure they have now reached. If it is true- [DOT]land I have no reason to doubt it; indeed I was astonished at the statement-that water carriage to-day is practically equal mile for mile to land carriage, then surely there is something wrong. And if it is equally true that for what cost $7.50 before the war $25 is charged to-day, unquestionably there is an opening for some remedy, even if we do go the length of providing competition by our own investment. I do not pretend to have any experience in the cattle business, but knowing as I do the conditions under which the cattle men lived before the war, when the rate was $7.50, it is inconceivable that the industry could exist under a $25 rate.

That is why I am anxious to
provide a remedy.

I am not complaining of that, but it is an awful start to make to send Mr. W. T. R. Preston over and make the provision for him the first charge against the campaign. The minister's own efforts may result in something, and we hope they will. Could he not give us an indication as to what he proposes to do? There is no reason why

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that could not be done; no time would be so suitable for him to do so as the present. I am not anxious to discuss the matter to-night but we would have this advantage, that we could come to the discussion much better informed if we had an intimation in advance as to what the nature of the proposed legislation is.
I would hardly care to discuss the matter without first having considered it fully with my colleagues.

The Minister of the
Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) told us a while ago that there was to be something, so that he evidently knows about it.

It is 12.20 p.m. now and we have been working hard all day. During the past few days the House has been adjourning around 1 o'clock in the morning. This item is not large but it is an important one and it could stand further discussion. If the minister is not familiar with Mr. Preston's record perhaps a little more information could be given him if the item were allowed to stand.
I do not like to make statements I am not sure of, but I do know something of what has been already stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland), and I feel confident that if the minister wants more information regarding Mr. Preston's record it can be got. Certainly it does not seem to me that Mr. Preston is the right man to send on a mission of this importance. If his investigations lead to nothing I doubt whether the members from the West will feel satisfied with any report he might make. I rose however to suggest that having in view the lateness of the evening this item might stand. The minister has made good progress and unless he wants to keep us until two o'clock he should report progress.

I would hardly
think it possible that the minister would adopt the attitude he has taken in view of the statements that have been made regarding IMr. W. T. R. Preston. Transportation, not only inland but on the ocean, presents great difficulties from the standpoint of rates; the rates are absolutely prohibitive. Unless something is done therefore I do not know what the outcome is going to be for agriculture. If the minister insists on retaining Mr. Preston in his service I am going to move that the item be reduced by as large a figure as possible. Unless we have an assurance that the services of this gentleman are going to be utilised in some capacity in the interests of the country I will not be a party to voting this item. In view of the attitude of
the government therefore I move that the item now before the committee be reduced by $9,999.

Just a word on the amendment. Is it the wish of this committee that the expenses of the Imperial Shipping Committee which visited this country to investigate freight rates on the ocean shall not be paid? If this' vote is not passed there will be no means of paying those expenses. I propose carrying on an investigation with one object in view namely to secure if possible some reduction in the rates on cattle and other commodities going from Canada to the United Kingdom. Supply-Trade and Commerce

If $2,000 is required for this
other sendee, the amount apparently voted to Mr. Preston would be $4,600. If my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) could see his way clear to' make a change in his figures, I would be pleased that the amount to be voted should be the $2,000, and that $4,600 should be struck off.

There is no fixed amount for
Mr. Preston; he may be in England for another month, he may not be. If he returns to Canada before I leave I shall be very gkd.	j|,t(

I appreciate that; but the
minister has explained that of this $10,000 $2,000 is required for a specific purpose, and that the balance may or may not be required for a specific purpose, and that the balance may or may not be required for Mr. Preston. The vote is for two-thirds of $10,000, which would be $6,600. If the $2,000 is required for the building, that would leave a vote of $4,600, which would be devoted possibly-we will put it that way-to Mr. Preston.

Roughly speaking, he has an
allowance of about $25 a day including expenses, which would be not more than $750 a month. If he is away, say, four months, the amount paid him will not be over $3,000.

Is it not a fact that the
Imperial Shipping Committee intervenes in complaints between shippers and shipowners; and has the Dominion a representative on that committee?
That is true.
Mho is the Dominion's representative?
Mr. Larkin.

While the Imperial Shipping Committee apparently (were effective in reducing rates, yet it seems to me that their action was effective only so far as the millers were concerned, because the cattle rate instead of being brought down even with the low rate was raised to make it on a par with the high rate. So it seems to me the commission did not accomplish very much. But why was not this matter of the cattle shipper presented to the committee when it visited Canada? i understand that at Winnipeg the evidence relating to the cattle trade was taken under protest, the chairman stating that the committee had received no instructions to investigate the cattle trade. The cattle rates having been a matter of con-[The Chairman.]
tention for a good many years, I should like to know wrhy this committee was brought over here at considerable expense to investigate the grain business, while the cattle business was not touched.

I have already stated that the committee w>as asked to investigate the cattle rates as well as the grain rates. If my hon. friend will drop into my office to-morrow I shall be very glad to show him the letter of instructions which was addressed to the chairman of the Imperial Shipping Committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, in
view of the statement made by the minister that $2,000 of this vote has been expended for another purpose, and that the vote is for two-thirds of the amount appearing in the Estimates, with the consent of the committee I should like to change the figures in the motion now before the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That cannot be done; the amendment must be withdrawn and a new amendment moved. The question is on the amendment, which has been already read to the committee. Does the hon. member have the unanimous consent of the committee to withdraw this amendment?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment is
withdrawn.

Will the minister not accept
the suggestion we made? It is now thirty-two minutes past twelve. We have done a good day's business.
We have been discussing this all evening. I am willing to abide by the decision of the committee.

Usually the minister is in
charge of matters of this kind. We want to be fair to him, but I think lie is getting on well. Surely he does not want to keep us here all night.
We might as well decide now.
Question.

I move that the
item now before, t'he committee be reduced by $4,000.

Is the hon. gentleman
(Mr. Sutherland) in favour of the principle of an inquiry into ocean freight rates?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Most assuredly I
am, but I do not see any reason for employing a man of the reputation of W. T. R. Preston to make an inquiry of that kind. There are many competent men in the department who have all the knowledge required to make such an investigation. I doubt whether a trip across the ocean is necessary to secure the information that is required. I am satisfied that the minister, with his business acumen and the officers in his department can very quickly obtain all the necessary information without employing a character of this kind. Mr. W. T. R. Preston's whole record is against the utilization of his services in this capacity.
What particular charge does the hon. member make against Mr. W. T. R. Preston?

I cannot make it
any clearer than I have already made it. I gave a partial report of his history for the past twenty-five years. It has been placed on the records of this House time and again.

The charges made by the
hon. gentleman have been very general in their form. Nobody in this assembly this evening has been able to determine what the hon. member means by those charges. Let him make a specific charge against Mr. Preston.

Surely the charge
made by the candidate in West Elgin, Mr. McNish, should be sufficient.

Did the law proceed against him. Was action taken against him? Was anything proved against him? Nothing at all. I have known W. T. R. Preston for a number of years. I knew other organizers in Ontario who are dead and buried, but I am not one of those who wish to stir up the embers of the past. W. T. R. Preston is one of the cleverest men in Ontario. He may have been guilty, although not proven guilty, of indiscretions in elections he took part in. He was organizer for the Liberal party for a great many years and an abler man in that capacity never occupied the position. I can make charges against men, and prove them, too, who were organizers for the Conservative party, but that is not my province, nor is it my determination in getting up here to-night. But I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland) to explain why in the election of 1917 in the Old Country W. T. R. Preston was arrested and kept in custody all day on a trumped up charge and released in the evening to prevent his activities during that day? Then I would like
to ask the hon. gentleman to produce a booklet or pamphlet written by W. T. R. Preston entitled "Taking off the Lid," making serious charges in regard to that election across the pond, charges which have never been answered to this day, though they were broadcast through the length and breadth of Ontario, and although they have been in the hands of hon. gentlemen apposite for a number of years?
I have never seen it.
These charges have never been answered. One can therefore understand the animosity toward W. T. R. Preston on the part of hon. gentlemen in that corner of the House to-night.

I had just one object in investigating the ocean rates. I selected Mr. Preston to do the preliminary work. He has been at it for the last six weeks or two months, and now by your amendment you ask the committee to repudiate the action of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If this vote does not carry there will be nothing to pay Mr. Preston. He has to be paid, but I am willing to stand behind the vote of the committee and will allow hon. members to decide whether I am taking the proper course in investigating the ocean rates at present in effect.

I do not need to make
any comment on the minister's statement except this:	His argument, if there was one,
was to the effect that the government, having employed this man without the authority of parliament, now must have the money to pay him, no matter whether the government's action was proper or not. Parliament, if it has any authority at all, will exercise it in this case. As to the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. McKay) I do not think I am in a position to dispute that there is a measure of cleverness in W. T. R. Preston. I will concede also that for the purposes for which he was appointed as Liberal organizer he probably worked hard and had some qualifications; but I shall not define those qualifications. As to his being arrested in England, I did read about it. He was arrested by an army officer who, I understand, did not know who he was, and thought he was making a nuisance of himself. I did see the pamphlet that he wrote. He wrote it for the purposes of the Liberal convention, whereupon the Liberal convention passed a resolution that they wanted to get into power in order to investigate the charges of W. T. R. Preston, in order to investigate the awful scandals that he said had been perpetrated in England. They got into power by the storm they raised and

Supply-Trade and Commerce
under the dust they created, but they never investigated the charges. They have been two and a half years in office now, but they have shuddered at the brink. Now we have them in front of us; I want them to investigate the W. T. R. Preston charges. I want them to send a commissioner who is a commissioner to England to investigate them. Hon. gentlemen will remember that the worst of the charges were made against men who now are their closest friends. Catch them investigate the charges! Why, if the hon. member for North Renfrew came here with forks and tongs he could not prod them into it. So let the hon. gentleman not refer to charges that his own party are afraid to investigate. Preston's record smells to high Heaven in this province. As respects a matter of this importance, a matter that demands experience of a quality that he is foreign to as a stranger in the Dominion, this item is nothing but an outrage on the treasury and it is an insult to parliament to ask to have it voted.

I am sorry that a subject of so much importance to this country cannot be discussed without charges being hurled from one side to the other. We have tried to-night to talk business, serious business, business which affects our people and their getting a living. Speaking for my friends around me, I think I can say that we do not propose to take any part in the washing of old, dirty political linen. I am sorry we cannot talk business without that being brought in.
It does not matter who is appointed?

I am glad to see that all
parts of the House realize the importance of this subject, and the responsibility for this appointment must be on the government.

It rests with us if we
vote the money.

I do not know what the
qualifications of Mr. Preston are, and I asked the minister. I really think he might have been better advised if he had appointed Mr. Duncan Marshall. He has a knowledge of the subject at any rate, but I know that if he had been appointed hon. gentlemen to my right would have raised just as great a storm of protest as they are doing over this appointment.

We sent him over
to the Old Country three times last year.
I know what is said about him, but I repeat, he has a knowledge of this particular subject.

Better than Preston, all
right.

Yes, but in my opinion the
responsibility for this appointment must rest on the government. I believe the money should be voted for this inquiry, and I am not going to support the amendment.

The responsibility does
not rest on the government alone. It rests upon everybody who votes for the item. Members need not be afraid that I am going at this hour to discuss Mr. Preston. I know very little about him anyway. But just assume that this government appointed a criminal from the penitentiary; I am not going to suggest that Mr. Preston is in that class at all, but suppose the government took a criminal out of the penitentiary and sent him over. Listening to what my hon. friend from Saltcoats has just said, that would be all right, the government had the power to do it; the responsibility be on the government, and then he votes to pay the money for something that he might not in private life say he would approve of, just because the government had done it. Can truckling go further?

I would just like to
make one comment in reply to what my hon. friend from St. John has just said. The only evidence we members in this corner of the House have had so far as to Mr. Preston's alleged bad character has come from the gentlemen to my right. Now I have a great deal of respect for these gentlemen, particularly for some of them, but I have not been encouraged from what experience I have had in the past to take all their statements at their full face value, and unless I have other evidence to back up their statements, I do not propose to take them at their full face value. If there was other definite evidence apart from the statements that have been made which would go to prove something against Mr. Preston, and not merely statements on the floor of this House by men who, however honourable, are not without a slight tincture of partisan feeling, I would accept that evidence and vote against the appointment of an unsuitable man.

Does the hon. member
consider it no evidence when a letter is read signed by the man himself, in which he urges the bringing out of foreign immigrants and keeping them, one hundred families in a county, for the purpose of keeping control of them and influencing an election?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I am prepared to
accept a written document of that kind1 at its face value. It was written, I understand, about twenty years ago. That man may have been a good Liberal organizer at that time, but that does not necessarily prove to me that he is not fairly honest in his business dealings.

He was not a Liberal
organizer at that time. At the time he wrote the letter he was a Commercial agent for the Dominion, and was paid a salary by the Dominion government.

Has the letter which
was read, or have his actions which have been condemned, any bearing on his qualifications for investigating the cattle trade? If it were proved that this man were unsuitable I would take a chance on destroying the investigation by refusing to vote the money, but as it is I am not prepared to accept the statements at their face value. In spite of the gentlemanly remarks of the hon. member for St. John, somewhat characteristic of him, I am not prepared to accept his word, and I propose to take a gambling chance in voting $4,000 that the government is sufficiently alive to the sense of their responsibility to see that a man is appointed who has some qualifications, and I propose instead of destroying the possibility of any investigation, to vote for the item.

I am afraid my hon. friend is fairly easily satisfied. If he is anxious to acquire some information with regard to Mr. Preston I would refer him to Hansard of July 26, 1899, page 8579, and of April 4, 1907.

When have you been
studying that?
This is 1924.

Afterwards, while
Mr. Preston was in the employ of the federal government he was a Liberal organizer for the province of Ontario.

Was he engaged in the
1917 election?

He took an active
part in the election overseas, and I only wish I had some of the literature over his signature that he circulated among the soldiers overseas, because if there was ever damning literature against any man it is the literature circulated by W. T. R. Preston on that occasion.

Look in your back pocket.
You might find it there.
Amendment negatived; yeas 13, nays, 41.

Item agreed to.
Inspection and Sales Act, administration of, $3,000.

If the minister purposes
going on now, I may as well warn him he will go on in vain.

I move that the committee
rise and report progress, but I wish to say that I did not like the threat of my right hon. friend.
-It should not have been necessary.

If my right hon. friend had waited a moment he would have heard me move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
